Interview with Bauza
Cassette 1-2
December 13, 1978

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
-- where you were born and how you got into music.

Well, I born in Havana April 28, 1911. I started to study music at age five, when my godfather started teaching me some (inaudible), and then I went to the Conservatory, Havana Music Conservatory, and I study s through (inaudible), harmony, and I went to the clarinet, studied clarinet for nine years.

Then I had four year piano. Then I went, I joined a Havana philharmonic orchestra as a bass clarinet, and from there (inaudible) playing with different dance bands (inaudible) typical dance, the beguine, playing clarinet.
Can you describe what the instrumentation of that typical band was at the time?
Well, during the time, when I first started playing, the first band that I played, that's what they called a typica. Typica consists in two clarinets, a brass instrument they call figli --
Which is a what?
What is no known in this country, is from the European countries.
But is it --
No, it's like a -- it's like a euphonia or something like that, and that -- in that vein.
Like a baritone.

Like a baritone, like. And they used to use a bass trombone, cornet, figli and big (inaudible) and a (inaudible) -- that was a typica, what they call a typica. That was the popular hands in Cuba when I first started to play.
This was about 19 when?
This was around 1920, '21, around there, '21, '22. And then they came what they called the chiranga orchestra. The chiranga orchestra was piano, flute, violin, bass, a small tymbali and guiro.
Uh-huh. And you were playing with the typica, right?

I played the typica first, and then the chiranga came in -- be popular because the sound of chiranga's more for small places and for homes -- and the typica was too loud, only can play in open places. You know what I mean. So it was then the chiranga replaced the typica.
The last typica orchestra is (inaudible) complete in 1933, no later, already was in here already.
Right.
In 1927 I came here to record for Victor with the Orchestra Antonio Maria Romeo.
This was in New York.
That was in New York. That was the first
chiranga orchestra. It was the best orchestra at that time in Cuba.
What were you playing?

I was playing triangle. Then, when I got here, I went to the Paramount Theater, to the -- Paul Weinman. They just got through playing the Rhapsody in Blue. And my friend in love with the saxophone. Franco Jobai used to play the saxophone. So I brought my saxophone. We went back to Cuba, and 15 day after we recorded, we went to Cuba. So I started playing my saxophone.
Let me just check the --
(Recording interruption.)
Good. So we know we're in good shape. Okay. So you went back, and you started playing. Was this the C melody sax?
I bought an alto saxophone. I bought an also saxophone. And I started buying records from here. In those days Red Nichols was very popular there.
With the Five Pennies.

With the Five Pennies. And I feel in love with that orchestra, and I used to buy all their records when they used to come out and try to, you know, try to get acquainted with the -- with the jazz, and I was fascinated with the way those guys played, and then I was trying to do it with my clarinet, what the clarinet player used to do there.
And then there was, well, the bands like Murphy Five. It was a different band --
What was that, the --
Murphy Five, they used to call them.
And that Red McCarthy biggest --
Yeah.
And different -- different band I used to buy records from. So I start play saxophone in the nightclub in Havana then already. And nowadays I develop pretty good idea what the jazz was.
Was this with a Cuban jazz group or--
Yeah, Cuban jazz group. Everybody was Cuban.
Right.
Yeah, was no American musician in Havana.
But were you playing exclusively jazz or a mixture?

Jazz, exclusively jazz. And the -- in the cabaret we play Tokyo Cabaret. It was strictly for tourists. They had a little one, what you call a jazz band and would play the jazz music and show and the typical Cuban set, that for the dance, for the people that, when they dance, they make the music.
And that -- my time -- I divide my time between that and the symphony orchestra. Then the thing got so hard for me,

you know, working until 4:00 o'clock in the morning, and we were -- in the symphony we always started about 10:00 o'clock in the morning. It was really hard. And there was no money involved with the symphony in those days in Cuba. It just -- was just more for prestige.

We get a little something, but I, you know, and I was getting good money in the nightclub. So I said, well, this is it. So I stay in the jazz scene, so much that everybody started raving about the way I play and I should come to United States. I was wasting my time in Cuba, you know. And I reached the top over there. So there was no other place to go.
Along came the show with broadcasting from the Cotton Club and the Duke Ellington Band. Now --
It came to Cuba.
Yeah, I used to listen on the short wave every night, Duke Ellington. Then I really went out of my mind. I say, I got to do it. I got to do it.
We're talking about what, now, 1928, '29?

That was in '29. No, that was 1929, '30, 1930. So in 1930, listening to this band, I made up my mind that I've got to come over. So one night I just got right up on the job, and I told the owner, say, well, this is my last night. I was working (inaudible) really, just (inaudible)
cabaret in Havana.

So the guy said, you're crazy. Why? You're making a hell of a money here. I say, well, I just -- I just want to advance myself. This is what I like, and I (inaudible) there. Some money -- I want to improve myself. So I came to New York.
I got into New York, and Duke Ellington was out of town. So I wait until the band got back. The day that --
To where -- I'm sorry?
He was traveling. Duke Ellington went to the road.
Right.

So I waited until they got back. And I never forget they opened Lafayette Theater. That was on Seventh Avenue and 132nd, 131st. That was when the -- the big Black shows, every week they had to deal with a new show, different orchestra.
This would be 1930 by now.
Yeah, in late '30s. I got into the theater when they opened at 9:00 o'clock in the morning. And I stay there until they finally show up (inaudible) that night.
They started back at 9:00 in the morning?
Well, the theater opened at 9:00. They used to do four shows a day, four, five shows a day. So I stayed All four days, just listening to the band. So one day I

I sat. I couldn't speak no English, but I used to go around the RHYTHM Club around the corner on 131st, and I used to go there every night, order me seats and hang around there. And they come in there, all the corner musicians, all the guys, you see, and if I come in there, you know, I had a hell of a time to -- to transmit myself to that.

But I mean, they just like a light, they had to lighten me. So I used to bring my saxophone around and play. You know what I mean. They -- and then a whole lot of those guys said, 'You play beautiful. You play beautiful saxophone.' The only thing, you got to develop more volume, because, you know, down there in Cuba they play soft music, you know.
And those great, big, heavy bands here, they would drown me. So --
Who were you -- who were you hanging out with?

Well, in those days the guys that hang around there were all like guys like Benny Carter, Jimmy Harrison, Red Allen, Lou Metcalf, Charlie Johnson, the Whitman brothers -- that used to play with Charlie Johnson -- Wilbur de Paris, Sidney de Paris, all the big musicians in those days, all the jazz musicians, all the guys from Procope, Johnny, from Fletcher Henderson, Jeffrey, Bozobelli (phonetic), all the biggest guys.
So you were getting another
(inaudible)?

I was -- hang around all day, and before I knew, I was speaking English. That I do know, because when -- no way for me to speak Spanish then. No Spanish people around here. You can hardly see one. So I have to either talk English or die.

So I begin to get acquainted with those guys. So I remember very -- my first job. A fellow, old man those days, used to be a very popular ragtime piano player called Luckey Roberts. He used to (inaudible), he used to play those swanky private parties for the rich people.

And then was another guy too, very popular those days, a big man, they called him Joe Jordan. He was a big conductor, writer. So he took me to play one Broadway show called "Fast and Furious." The show didn't last much time. But that was a different idea.
And then I started playing with Leroy Smith. He was a violin player from Philadelphia; violin player, very popular those days. (Inaudible). So from there I went to Noble Sissle orchestra.
Which would be when, what?
At Central Hotel.
Yeah, when?
That was around late '31. I'm in late '31 already.

Let me ask -- let me interject while I think of it, did -- did Luckey Roberts ever play anything with a Latin tinge to it, because back in 1914-15 he wrote a couple of very fine ragtime tangoes, and in 1939 he wrote the whole so called Spanish Suite.
Yeah, he used to play something like that when I come to -- when I come to see --
This was a period when Rhumba was first coming in, right? With Catsee (phonetic) and -- Aspiazu
No, the funny thing about this, they knew something about rhumba here and especially those musicians for down the -- down South way.
Right.

That was familiar, and the reason why they're familiar, because I've been reading now lately -- I've been reading so much in Cuba. There's a book coming out in Cuba now telling the whole history thing, the slave movement. The slave movement, they came. They stop in Luciana (phonetic). And from Luciana they ship some to Haiti, some to Santo Domingo, some to Cuba.
That's why the music has -- the music rings as African and West Indian, and that's where the jazz born, really, there too, that's where the Cuban music born too.
Right.
So we got the first music that was

played in Cuba then, was what you call in contradansa. The contradansa come from France. So the African musician and the new Cuban-born musician, they start playing the music, but they start putting that African rhythm into the thing, and before you know that really was so powerful that the contradansa lost something. But in the same time they got into something else.
That developed into the dance soon and the Cuban dance.
And before that (inaudible) --
And they are habanera (phonetic).
Right.
And when they are hardened, they sound more blues. He put the habanera touch in the verse of the St. Louis Blues.
Right. So -- but was Luckey Roberts playing -- because Aspersoo (phonetic) had --
Well, Aspersoo came in --
-- when I did?
Yeah, 1930.
In fact, I came together with him on the same boat.
Uh-huh. Did you -- did you hear the show that he played at Paramount and around?
*correctly- RKO PALACE.

Yeah, I remember it was -- the front of it was a shinga (phonetic). They just pass away, man, and in Spain, [Antonio] MACHIN, the pay machine (phonetic) was a close friend of mine. So that's how I came to be a trumpet player, after I (inaudible). Later on I became a trumpet player.
Anyway, I'm sorry. I got distracted because I'm thinking Lucky Roberts and Dick Dick Jazz Hangert (phonetic), but anyway, you -- you were starting to play duets and went to Noble Sissle in '31.

I went to Noble Sissle -- late '31, I went to Noble -- '32, in '32, I think. He used to play in the Florentine G-GRILL (phonetic) group, Park Center Hotel. They call it Park Sheraton today. So there I play -- he play like a kind of -- kind of society called a band with a match -- naturally they got a few good jazz numbers, because they had a guy like Sidney Gibbon (phonetic), Bechet, the soprano player.
Sidney Bechet.
Sidney Bechet. He was featured in that band.
Right.
They had a guy like Tommy Ladnier, trumpet player. He was a feature too. He (inaudible) them too, later.
Right.
And they had a -- they had Nat King
Cole's brother was playing the bass, June Cole, that and (inaudible) the kind of players that was in that band. They had a hell of a -- different guys.
So from there I stayed with that band maybe about three or four, five months (inaudible). something like that
Did you get to know Bechet and Ladnier?
Oh, yeah, I worked with them in there.
Right.

I worked with him (inaudible) and I played with him (inaudible), with Noble Sissle and then I left my job, and the guy that was working, that I was substituting, came back to the job. So (inaudible) Sam Wooding came from Paris, and as I was working around with Sam Wooding there was another big band (inaudible).

And I got out of work. Aspirin I started to went back to Cuba. Machin had a quartet. (Inaudible) it was a very popular quartet, record-wise. So the trumpet player, calling Chino (phonetic), left and went back to Cuba. So nobody around here that couldn't play that style, the trumpet he needed for his quartet.

So one day I was with him in his house and he was going -- he going crazy. I say, "Well, if you buy me a trumpet, I think I be able to do like that." He said, "You don't play trumpet." I said, "Well, I don't play no trumpet,

but I know the positions, and I think if I get it home, in a couple of weeks I'd be able to play what you want, because what you want is the idea, the idea (inaudible). All I got to get, the ambition."

So we went to the pawn shop, and we bought a horn for 15 bucks. So I fooled around with it. Well, after I was about a week with the horn, I went to the first rehearsal. The idea was there, but I used to miss whole lot of notes. He said, "Mari, I don't think you're going to be -- you don't have to record it in another three weeks." In another three week I be ready.
So it happened that way. Tried it, got it. The record came out fine.
What -- do you remember what the recording was?

The first number that I recorded with Machin, I can never forget, called La Parumbeda. I can never forget that time because it was my first time to record, and it was a hit song. So I keep messing around with the trumpet. Then I fall in love with trumpet, and I want to play like (inaudible) so bad I can taste it. So I got whole -- all his records, and I follow and play just like, you know, and copy and everything. All right.
So I got me a chance to fool around with the bands, small bands with the trumpet. I used to play gigs. I say, get a man on the trumpet, I get on the sax. I give up the sax

and play. I give the sax to a friend of mine. He come from Cuba, so I gave him my horn, take it. He had a contract to go to Paris with Rimac (phonetic) Brothers. Remack was a -- there was a band of father and son, and they used to have -- used to do vaudeville with a small, with about ten piece (inaudible) band.
And now they want to go to Europe. I just got here. I don't want to leave.
Was this a Cuban band or --
No, these guys -- Remack was --
Oh, Rimac.
Rimac.
Caesar Rimac.
Caesar Rimac. So --
They used to do that thing with the big doll.
That's it. So I give this job to this kid who just came from Cuba, sacrifice, I give him the job and give my horn to him. So I say now, I definitely bet you I'm a trumpet player now.

So there was a little band in the Palladium -- in the Savoy called the Hy Clark and his Missourians. They need a trumpet. And when I went there, they give me the job. It was a second-rate orchestra. But that's when I really got developed.
Was this a kind of an opening band (inaudible)?

It was one of those second-rate bands. They used them at the Savoy as a (inaudible) band, you know, so that chance to develop my playing and got better experience with the jazz and listen all these good men they used to play in there, those bass. You know what I mean? So I'm ready for everybody. So I practiced with that band around six or seven months. Chick Webb Cheat-Wook (phonetic) was working there all the time, in and out, in and out, in and out. So he used to listen to me. I don't have no idea I'm ever going to play with the -- because he always had you have the best in business and the bestest, and to me up to today I don't think there has been anybody better -- with better idea how to form an orchestra, how to play than him. He was (inaudible) musician because he got -- he got an ear, he had a conception about rhythm and the arrangement, how to play. There was nothing like it. For me there was nothing like it. So we had a trumpet player called Lou Bacon
it don't cost you nothing to go. In fact the man told me to tell you to go. So I said, all right, I'm going, sure.

I got there. There was about ten, 15, 20 trumpet players. Every -- these guys play maybe half a tune, a tune. This guy and all right -- so come my time, he say, who's to come in there -- say, INDIAN! in there, come in; it's your turn. So I start playing. I play (inaudible). He say, I want you to work tonight with me. I say, all right. So 10:00 o'clock we start. All right.

So I got in the Savoy that night. I'm nervous. I play, play all night. And so he said, you know, we're going to have rehearsal right after the job. You got half an hour to go and buy yourself a sandwich, you know. You come back. We're going to start rehearsal.

All right. So when I got back, I looked for the guys. Where's the guys? He said, no, never mind the guys, rehearsal for you. I said, for me? I never seen no rehearsal for one man (inaudible) that's the way I do with you. All right.

So he say, take such and such a number out. I took the number out. He said, play. He said, don't phrase that like that. So he used to hum to me the way he wanted me to phrase. I try. I said keep going. No. Like that -- I had good ideas.
So when we got through rehearsal about 5:00 o'clock

in the morning, I say, I don't think I'm the man, you know, to do what you got, what you need. You need a man here with experience. No, if you listen to me, you're the man I want. So all right. I come back to work the next day. Same thing. I say, Chick, I don't think I'm the man. I don't want to hold you back. You know what I mean? I appreciate you giving me this opportunity, but I don't want to hold you back. He said, no, no, no, no, you listen to me. All right. So by the third day, he say, the job is yours. So just listen to me, and that's that. I said all right.
So I begin to QUALMATE (inaudible) the man so much, and the music was so -- nothing around, not for me --
Can you talk a little about the music? I mean --

He used to have the best guys arranging for him. He used to go -- sometime he didn't have no money to pay his room because he had to pay the arrangement. He used to buy arrangements, the best arrangements for all kind of money, money he don't make himself.

But that was his idea. I want the best band. I want the best arrangements. I've got to go to the top, and (inaudible) but I'm going to be there. I've got to get there. He was right too, because every time he developed somebody, they take them away -- Fletcher and Duke and all that (inaudible). They was able to pay more money.

So I keep -- all right, I keep listening to the guy. About six months later, one day -- I never forget it -- he call rehearsal for the band. And that day everybody's seated on the stand. After work he say, fellows, I want to announce something today. Starting today the man in charge to call the shots, top of the band, the rest of the band is MariO. To me that was the biggest thing that ever happened in my life. And I didn't know what to do. I said, Chick, I said (inaudible). Go ahead and lead (inaudible).

So I started calling numbers (inaudible) got rehearsing. All right, everything went beautiful (inaudible) he got hold of some of the arrangement and call it (inaudible) listen this kid play all night. I want you to arrange a number for him, such and such a number.
Who was this again?

He called a different writer he used to have, a guy named Alexander. (Inaudible) in the band, Ron Alexander. (Inaudible) MariO, you may not get a chance. I say (inaudible) something and let me try. I'll get it in the rehearsal. Let me try. If the man like, you start, maybe he go give you work. So he made an arrangement for the band. He made "Liza." We recorded it. Chick went crazy.
He started getting work -- some -- order some for me, for me to play. He had another guy named Charlie Dixon used to write for him. Charlie wrote the hard stuff.
You were playing solo trumpet as well, were you?

All right. Yeah, you know, solo, my own style. He didn't want me to mess around with the jazz like the other trumpet player, because one day he said -- I told him -- he said, never mind that stuff you want to play with Louie. Never mind that. You've got to develop yourself into something else because, see, every Negro trumpet player can outplay you that kind of stuff, because that's their usual. They match you in that.

What I want you to do, do you hear those white trumpet players when they play jazz, like Red Nichols and (inaudible) they play around the melody. That's what I want you to do, what none of those guys do; they play something else. So that's what I want you to do, develop the very, start simple, you fool around with the melody, just little bit, jazz around the melody. Don't try to do that hard stuff because you won't outdo them.

They had a guy named Bobby Scott playing second (inaudible). He said, you aren't going to outdo those guys. So try to get a start like that. I've got three different styles in my trumpet section, and I'll be able to work my music different ways. All right, great.
So one day we work in the Apollo Theater, and a guy came to me, said, Mario, there's a girl that won the amateur

contest last night in Harlem Opera House, next door. She's a terrific singer, and I would like for you to take Chick up after her. Why don't you bring the girl here, and between the shows we'll go to the (inaudible), you know, in the parlor, the piano and hear her.

So this -- they brought that girl, and I listen to the a couple of songs this is the girl (inaudible) singer (inaudible). She's terrific. So I went to the dressing room, and I said, Chick, I just got through (unintelligible). He said, yeah? Bring her to me. So I brought the girl to the dressing room. When he saw the girl, he didn't want her. She had a bad appearance, you know. She was reggedy, you know (inaudible) right, but she sing like -- I said the appearance, we can fix that. Let me be the sponsor for that.

He was (inaudible) and we -- we're supposed to go up to the -- to play the college stage. We have three days at Yale University. In those days they used to feature, they used to bring to those campuses all the big jazz bands playing (inaudible) at universities (inaudible) began in this manner.

So I say, let's take Peggy, this girl (inaudible). He say, man -- I say, we take her to the beauty parlor. I'll take her to the beauty parlor. We'll get a nice evening gown. Let me worry about her. So he say all right. Go on.
We took this girl. We didn't have no music for her.

We faked that music, and that lady -- the people in the college those three days, nobody wanted dance. Somebody wanted hear music, but it was such a big hit. So right away -- open New York, three days. We got a hold of Alexander's arrangements. We start writing right in like CRAZY (inaudible) with this girl, boom, Ella Fitzgerald. That's the way it happened.
Then we go --
Can you remember what date it was when she first --
Well, Ella, I think Ella joined the band going to on May '34 '35, I think.
How old was she then?
Ella was around, no more than 17 years old, something like that (inaudible). I don't think so. And if I'm wrong with the dates, excuse me, because I'm very bad at dates.
Yeah, well, they can be checked.
That can be checked.
Right.

But, that was the whole idea. So, it the girl MADE gave me such a hit, it was unbelievable. And then this guy started writing for her, just write. He used to play the (inaudible) and arrange it for her to sing. Then she'd sing rag, she'd sing swings all right. So the band start doing like this. Then we're going to the radio. We start broadcasting

on NBC. We used to broadcast every day. We go to the studio. We have the Radio City, across from Radio City. They had what you called in those days (unintelligible) problem in there, and they're broadcasting too from the Savoy Ballroom too. So we was on the air practically every day. Boom! She go along fine. (Unintelligible) Benny Goodman (inaudible) they take him.
Somehow they make some kind of (inaudible), and they let her record accompanied by Benny Goodman, (Unintelligible). And so forth
So Ella recorded with Benny Goodman when, about '35?
We already -- '35 to '36 anyhow, yeah, around there, because Benny Goodman's band organized around '35, in '35, because --
Yeah, '34, I think. Their big thing was that radio show.

Yeah, '34, because we was working in the Casino de Paris. There was Ben Pollack and Chick, and Ben Pollack was playing -- Harry James play in there. (Unintelligible) was the drummer. Miller was the tenor. And Benny was getting his band together.
And now, I recommend to Benny -- I play trumpet for a guy. He used to call it Luis Garcia. Luis Garcia was a very popular popular trumpet player. He was with Whiteman for a while.
: Where did he come from?
He from Puerto Rico, but he look like a German, real white guy with blond hair.
: Puerto Rican.
Yeah, he used to be a (unintelligible). He went to (unintelligible) want to stay. I don't know. (Unintelligible) likes him. I don't know. So they got hold of somebody else.

So in the meantime Chick recommended Gene Krupa for the band, and I recommended Harry James. Well, getting around, that's the way he -- Benny start getting his men, and they used to rehearse in the Savoy. So they used to come in the Savoy one night a week at night to play right next to us (inaudible). He was trying to get the guys into a field where they see (inaudible).

So Benny Goodman, he -- and there was a big promotion, big promotion (unintelligible) the guys (unintelligible). So when they start talking about a swing and swing, and they (inaudible), and I said to me that's a gimmick. It's a title. It's a gimmick. Whoever (unintelligible) this new (inaudible) Benny Goodman the King of Swing, it's the same music we've been playing all along.
: I was going to ask you -- it seems sad that a lot of Goodman's success came from arrangements that he got from Fletcher Henderson, and he bought Fletcher
Henderson's book.

Yeah. The first guy that started writing for Goodman was Jimmy Mundy. He got some of their -- Fletcher and some of the Horace Henderson, I bet, finally made Henderson this band just write complete right to play for him. That was his idea. He wanted band like Henderson band, and he succeeded to have a hell of a -- he developed the best white jazz guys band in that era, but nothing (inaudible).

So they got so popular and so big with the Savoy Ballroom arrangement a battle of music - (unintelligible) Chick Webb and Benny Goodman. The biggest event of music has happened in the city of New York, up to moment opened that (unintelligible).

I'll never forget what I think was one of -- I don't (inaudible). I know they opened the door 4:00 o'clock in the afternoon, the Savoy. The music is supposed to start 9:00 o'clock, and by 6:00 o'clock have to come the police because nobody (unintelligible), but when I come to work that night, and Chick said to everybody, fellows, I don't have to tell you this is the biggest thing that's going to happen to us, tonight. Tonight we got to make history. Our future depends on tonight. So I don't want any excuses. I don't want nobody (unintelligible). I don't want nobody to miss; anybody do any little thing, don't look for me (unintelligible), because this my life, man.
All right. So Benny played. He played his first set.
You know, people went crazy, you know, that whole band.
Do you remember what he played?
Any (inaudible).
I don't know. He called it a set with closed that Big John Special.
"Big -- I"

"Big John Special." That tune was written by Horace Henderson. And I opened my second set (inaudible). We're hoping for the same note. The house came down. And I remember, when we finish that first number, Goodman's band didn't even come out -- the bandstand. And Harry James said to Bobby Starr, "I got my lesson." Bobby Starr used to play some solo, and that number was unbelievable.

So from then on -- that night, the whole night there was (inaudible) music. And I remember when they'd walk in, Tommy Dorsey said to -- I think it was Wood Osman (phonetic), I bet you son of a gun I'm going to solo Chick Webb and Benny Goodman to pieces. I said, well, just put your money on the barrel.

And all the big -- the biggest band leaders in the business was there that night. That was the biggest thing that ever happened in the Savoy Ballroom. See, that band played like it never played before.
And Chick played so much drum that night, Gene Krupa jump in there (inaudible). He want to drum, and he -- that

band really played that night. Chick had a hell of a band in those days. Some of the band -- then the band started depending on playing -- and Ella Fitzgerald. Then you go to these funky places. The band started getting commercial, played the jazz here (inaudible) one number in the different bands. They want to get into the hotel kick (inaudible). They went to the hotel. They want to (Inaudible) the Paramount Theater. They went there, you know, then begin to do things, big things, going to Chicago to the Oriental Theater go to California (inaudible), you know.
We're talking about what, '37?
Yeah, we're in '37 now, right in '37.
When did you first record with Ella Fitzgerald?
